local_scope: Skimmed content/fair-trial-and-reliability-doctrines/index.md and node pages only for terminology, theories, and seed cases. Candidate existence checked before row inclusion against standalone content/cases files, _overhaul2/lake/_manifest.json by caption/party variant, _run/s6-candidates/r7-queue-batch1.jsonl, and _run/s6-candidates/gated.jsonl.
inclusion_floor: Rows are page candidates only when the missing case is controlling SCOTUS, a SCOTUS split-resolver, or directly controlling for officer field conduct, admissibility/suppression, or officer civil liability. Trial-craft-only confrontation/harmless-error material was not promoted.
source_note: Discovery and cross-checking used web sources only and no CourtListener. SCOTUS rows use Supreme Justia, LOC U.S. Reports PDFs, Oyez, Wikipedia snippets, or official Supreme Court docket/opinion pages as non-CourtListener sources.

caption: Rochin v. California
justification: Missing controlling due-process/admissibility case for officer field conduct: evidence obtained by conscience-shocking police conduct, including forcible stomach pumping, cannot be used consistently with due process. Useful as the substantive-due-process field-conduct ancestor to later reliability and suppression limits.

caption: Killian v. United States
justification: Missing controlling evidence-preservation precursor: good-faith destruction of preliminary FBI notes under normal practice did not itself require relief once the final reports were produced. It supplies adverse/limiting authority for officer report-note preservation before Trombetta and Youngblood.

caption: Moore v. Illinois
justification: Missing controlling eyewitness-identification/right-to-counsel case: a post-charge preliminary-hearing identification was a critical-stage confrontation at which counsel was required. No standalone case page was present; only a cross-reference appeared inside the existing Kirby page.

caption: United States v. Valenzuela-Bernal
justification: Missing controlling government-handling-of-defense-witnesses case: deportation of potential alien witnesses violates due process/compulsory-process principles only when the defendant makes a plausible showing that the lost testimony would have been material and favorable. Fits the officer/government field-conduct and reliability remit, not trial craft.

caption: Briscoe v. LaHue
justification: Missing controlling officer-civil-liability boundary: police officers who testify as witnesses in criminal trials have absolute witness immunity from 1983 damages claims based on alleged perjury. This is an adverse reliability/liability rule for officer testimony claims, not a trial-technique issue.

caption: California v. Trombetta
justification: Missing controlling due-process evidence-preservation anchor: the government must preserve evidence only when its exculpatory value was apparent before destruction and the defendant cannot obtain comparable evidence by other reasonably available means. Directly governs officer evidence-handling/admissibility questions.

caption: Arizona v. Youngblood
justification: Missing controlling evidence-preservation case for potentially useful evidence: absent police bad faith, failure to preserve potentially useful evidence does not deny due process. This is the key officer evidence-handling adverse rule paired with Trombetta.

caption: Illinois v. Fisher
justification: Missing controlling Youngblood application: bad faith is still required for failure to preserve potentially useful evidence even when the evidence is central to the defense and was destroyed after a pending discovery request. Party-name pre-check found only unrelated Michigan v. Fisher in the manifest/content set.

caption: Rehberg v. Paulk
justification: Missing controlling officer/official civil-liability witness-immunity boundary: grand-jury witnesses, including a government investigator, receive the same absolute immunity from 1983 claims as trial witnesses. Complements Briscoe for false-testimony liability limits outside trial-craft doctrine.

caption: McDonough v. Smith
justification: Missing controlling fabricated-evidence civil-liability split-resolver: a 1983 fabricated-evidence claim accrues when the criminal proceedings terminate in the plaintiff's favor. The Court resolved the Second Circuit's earlier-accrual rule against the favorable-termination approach used by the Fifth, Sixth, and Ninth Circuits and noted related Third Circuit authority.
